## A Note on Taper Anxiety and Cardio Creep

Warn the client explicitly about **cardio creep** — the very common tendency during a taper to add extra sessions, extend walks, or convince herself that she needs more movement because she feels restless and full of energy. This impulse comes from a good place but acts against the goal. The energy she feels is fatigue leaving the body and fitness consolidating. Adding work at this stage is like withdrawing money from a savings account the day before a large purchase. The account is full. Leave it alone.

If the anxiety becomes significant — and for some athletes it does — redirect it into productive non-physical activities: reviewing meet logistics, visualisation practice, organising equipment, planning the meet-day meal, or simply talking through the plan with you as her trainer. The conversation itself is often enough to settle the nervous system.

The cardio sessions above are the ceiling, not a floor. On any given day, if the client feels genuinely fatigued or flat, the correct decision is to skip the cardio session entirely and rest. **Rest is always the right answer when in doubt during a peak.**

## Bench Cue Management in a Peak Block
### The Shoulder Retraction Question

---

## The Short Answer

**Leave the cue alone. Do not drill it. Do not change it.**

If she has been using this cue throughout the accumulation block and her bench has been moving well, then that cue is already wired into her motor pattern. It is part of her lift. Treating it as something that needs corrective drilling in the final three weeks introduces exactly the kind of technical uncertainty that derails peaking blocks — not because the cue is wrong, but because the timing of the intervention is.

---

## The Longer Answer

There is an important distinction to make here between two very different situations, and the right course of action depends entirely on which one applies.

**Situation A — The cue is working and the lift looks good.**

She found this cue herself during accumulation, it has become automatic, and her bench is technically sound and progressing. In this case the cue is not really a cue anymore — it is a movement. It has been practised enough times that conscious thought about pulling the shoulders together has become unconscious execution of a stable upper back position. Drilling it now adds nothing and risks making her overthink a pattern that is already grooved. Leave it completely alone. If anything, affirm it — tell her the upper back position looks solid and that she should trust what she has built.

**Situation B — The cue is compensatory and creating a problem you can see.**

She has been over-cueing the retraction, creating excessive anterior shoulder stress, an inconsistent touch point, or a position that looks forced rather than natural. The lift has a visible technical flaw that this cue may be masking or causing. In this case you still do not drill a correction in a peaking block — but you do need to manage it carefully so it does not cost her white lights on meet day.

---

## How to Assess Which Situation You Are In

Watch her bench on Day 1 of Week 1 — the 3 × 3 at 80%. You are looking for four things specifically.

**First, the touch point.** Is it consistent set to set? Does the bar land in the same place on her sternum or lower chest every rep, or does it drift? An over-retracted shoulder position often causes the bar to travel too low or creates an inconsistent arc.

**Second, the shoulder position under load.** As the weight increases across the warm-up sets, do the shoulders stay retracted and depressed, or does one or both begin to roll forward or elevate? A cue that holds at 60% but breaks down at 85% is a cue that is masking instability rather than creating it.

**Third, the leg drive and full-body tension.** Shoulder retraction does not exist in isolation — it is part of the whole-body setup. If the retraction is solid, you should see it reinforcing the arch and the leg drive, not fighting against them.

**Fourth, her face and her breathing.** This sounds soft but it is genuinely useful. If she is consciously thinking hard about pulling her shoulders together on every single rep at 80%, you will see it — a slight pause before unracking, a particular expression of concentration, a breath held at the wrong moment. If the cue has become automatic, the setup will look fluid and the face will be calm.

If you watch the Week 1 bench sessions and everything looks like Situation A, you have your answer and you never raise the subject again until after the meet.

---

## If You Are in Situation B — The Peaking Block Management Strategy

Do not attempt to replace the cue with a different cue. Do not introduce new language around the shoulder position. What you can do, very carefully and very briefly, is **simplify rather than correct.**

Instead of telling her to think about something different, reduce the cognitive load of the existing cue. If she is over-cueing — pulling so hard that the position becomes rigid or forced — a single quiet phrase in the warm-up is sufficient: *"Set it and forget it. Find the position in the setup, then stop thinking about it."* This is not a technical correction. It is permission to trust the pattern she has already built rather than actively managing it through every rep.

Say it once in Week 1. Do not repeat it as a constant reminder. If you repeat it every session it becomes a new source of anxiety rather than a release of the old one.

---

## The Broader Principle for This Block

Peaking blocks are not the time to fix technique. They are the time to **express** technique. Every cue, every correction, every piece of coaching feedback you give in these three weeks should be in service of confidence and automaticity — not improvement. Improvement is a Week 1-through-10 project. It is finished now.

The lifts she brings to the meet are the lifts she has. Your job as her coach in these three weeks is to make sure she believes in those lifts completely, executes her setup with zero hesitation, and walks onto the platform feeling like the training has prepared her for exactly this moment — because it has.

Save the shoulder retraction conversation, the technique audit, and any cue refinements for the training block that begins after the meet. Write yourself a note now so you do not forget it. Then put it away until she has her total on the board.

# Meet Day Morning
### Full Timeline, Warm-Up Protocol, and Opener Execution

---

## The Governing Principle

Meet day morning is not the time for decisions. Every choice that can be made in advance should already be made — what she eats, what she wears, what she lifts, what she tells herself when she steps on the platform. Your job as her trainer in the days before the meet is to reduce the number of things she has to think about on the day itself to as close to zero as possible. The athlete who walks into the warm-up room with a clear plan and a calm mind will almost always outperform the athlete who is making it up as she goes, regardless of who is stronger on paper.

What follows is a complete morning framework. Adjust the specific times to fit the actual meet schedule once you have the flight order and attempt board information. The structure and the spacing are what matter — the clock times are placeholders.

---

---

## The Night Before

This is technically not meet day morning but it determines everything about how the morning feels, so it belongs here.

**By 9:00 PM — Equipment check, final and complete.**

Lay everything out physically. Singlet, belt, shoes, knee sleeves, wrist wraps, chalk if permitted, spare chalk, meet registration confirmation, handler credentials if applicable, water bottle, food bag. Check the federation rulebook one final time for any equipment specifications — stitching rules on singlets, knee sleeve length, belt width. Do this tonight so that a missing item discovered at 10 PM is a minor inconvenience rather than a 5 AM crisis.

**Dinner — familiar, carbohydrate-forward, low fibre.**

A meal she has eaten before. Pasta, rice, potatoes, bread — whatever she digests well and enjoys. Moderate protein. Low fibre to minimise any gastrointestinal activity during the meet. No alcohol. No new restaurant. No heroic portion sizes — comfortable and satisfying, not stuffed.

**In bed by 10:00–10:30 PM.**

She will probably not sleep perfectly. That is completely normal and will not meaningfully affect performance — one night of slightly disrupted sleep before a competition has a negligible effect on strength output. What matters is that she is horizontal, resting, and not scrolling through her phone until 1 AM. If sleep does not come easily, slow breathing exercises — four counts in, hold four, out four — will lower heart rate and cortisol without requiring her to actually fall asleep. Rest is the goal, not unconsciousness.

---

---

## Meet Day Morning Timeline

The following assumes a **9:00 AM first attempt** for the first flight. Work backwards from your client's actual first squat attempt to set the real times. The intervals between steps are what matter.

---

### 5:30 AM — Wake Up
### *(3.5 hours before first attempt)*

Wake up at least 3 to 3.5 hours before the first attempt. This is non-negotiable. The body needs time to fully activate — core temperature rises, the nervous system comes online, digestion processes the pre-meet meal, and the psychological shift from sleep to competition mode happens gradually rather than in a panic. Athletes who wake up 90 minutes before their opener and rush through everything perform below their capability not because they are weak but because their body has not had time to arrive.

A brief note on nerves at this moment: waking up with a racing heart and immediate anxiety about the day is extremely common and is not a bad sign. It means the competition matters and the body is beginning to mobilise resources. Acknowledge it, do not fight it, and move through the morning routine.

---

### 5:45 AM — Pre-Meet Meal
### *(approximately 3 hours before first attempt)*

This meal should be something she has eaten before training many times. Not a new food, not a special meet-day meal she has been saving — a familiar meal that her digestive system knows exactly what to do with.

**Composition:**
- **Carbohydrates — the priority.** 80–120 grams of easily digestible carbohydrate. Oats with honey and banana, white rice with a small amount of protein, toast with eggs and jam, a bagel with peanut butter. Whatever she has been eating before her heaviest training sessions.
- **Protein — moderate.** 25–35 grams. Eggs, Greek yoghurt, a protein shake alongside the carbohydrates. Enough to prevent any hunger during the meet but not so much that digestion is still active when she steps on the platform.
- **Fat — minimal.** Fat slows gastric emptying. Keep it low this morning. This is not the meal for avocado, full-fat dairy, or a large amount of nut butter.
- **Fibre — minimal.** Same logic. No high-fibre cereals, no large quantities of vegetables, no beans.
- **Fluids.** 500–750 ml of water with the meal. Begin the day hydrated.

Eat calmly. Sit down. Do not rush the meal. If appetite is suppressed by nerves — which is common — eat anyway, even if the portions are smaller than usual. The body needs the fuel regardless of what the stomach is telling her.

---

### 6:15 AM — Travel and Arrival
### *(aim to arrive at the venue 2–2.5 hours before first attempt)*

Arrive early enough that logistics do not create stress. Registration, equipment check, finding the warm-up room, locating the bathrooms, understanding the flight schedule, meeting the expediter — all of this takes time and all of it is easier when there is no rush. Arriving with time to spare allows the nervous system to settle into the environment rather than arriving already activated by the stress of being late.

On arrival, do the following in order:

**Register and complete equipment check** if not done the day before. Get this administrative task out of the way immediately so it is not hanging over the warm-up.

**Find the warm-up room and identify the equipment.** Note the bar — is it a stiff bar or a competition bar with more whip? Is the platform surface the same as training? Are the squat stands adjustable and how do they work? Familiarity with the environment reduces cognitive load during the warm-up itself.

**Locate the attempt board and understand the flight system.** Know how many lifters are in the flight, roughly how long each flight takes, and who the expediter is. The expediter is the most important person in the building for the next several hours — introduce yourself, be friendly, and confirm the communication protocol for submitting attempts.

**Find a quiet space and sit down for ten minutes.** Do nothing. Drink water. Let the environment become familiar. This deliberate pause before the warm-up begins is something experienced competitors do instinctively and inexperienced competitors skip entirely. Do not skip it.

---

### 7:15 AM — General Warm-Up
### *(approximately 90 minutes before first attempt, or when the flight before hers begins)*

The general warm-up is not the barbell warm-up. It is the transition from resting body temperature to training-ready body temperature. It should take 10–12 minutes and should feel like the beginning of any normal training session.

**Minutes 1–4: Light cardiovascular activation.**
Five minutes on a stationary bike if one is available in or near the warm-up room, or a brisk walk around the venue. The goal is simply to raise core temperature and begin increasing blood flow to the working muscles. Heart rate to 100–110 bpm — nothing more.

**Minutes 5–8: Dynamic mobility sequence.**
Move through this sequence deliberately but without rushing.
- Leg swings front-to-back, 10 per leg
- Leg swings side-to-side, 10 per leg
- Hip circles, 10 per direction
- Bodyweight squat, 10 reps — slow descent, pause at the bottom, focus on position
- Thoracic rotation in a half-kneeling position, 8 per side
- Shoulder circles, 10 per direction
- Band pull-aparts if a band is available, 15 reps
- Doorway or strap chest stretch, 30 seconds per side

**Minutes 9–12: Neural activation.**
Two or three explosive bodyweight movements to begin waking up the nervous system.
- Vertical jump, 5 reps — not for height, just for the feeling of fast, powerful muscle contraction
- Broad jump, 3 reps
- Clap push-up or fast push-up, 5 reps

This sequence is not glamorous and it is not complicated. Its job is simply to ensure that the first barbell warm-up set does not feel like it is coming from a cold start.

---

### 7:30 AM — Squat Warm-Up
### *(begins when the flight before hers is approximately halfway through, or 45–60 minutes before her first attempt)*

**The timing of the squat warm-up is the most technically demanding logistical task of the day.** The goal is to complete the final warm-up single approximately 5–8 minutes before she walks onto the platform for her opener. Too early and the nervous system activation fades; too late and she is still breathing hard when her name is called. Getting this right requires knowing the pace of the flight — roughly how many minutes per lifter — and working backwards from the expected time of her first attempt.

As a general rule of thumb: **one lifter takes approximately 2–3 minutes** including the attempt, the changeover, and the loading. A flight of 10 lifters therefore takes roughly 25–35 minutes per lift. Use this to estimate timing and adjust in real time.

**Squat warm-up sequence:**

All percentages are of her competition opener weight, which is itself approximately 90–92% of training max.

| Set | Load | Reps | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Empty bar | 5 | Full competition setup — walk out, commands, rack. Every rep. |
| 2 | ~40% of opener | 3 | Add weight in comfortable jumps. |
| 3 | ~55% of opener | 2 | |
| 4 | ~67% of opener | 2 | Belt goes on here if she uses one. |
| 5 | ~78% of opener | 1 | Knee sleeves on. Full equipment. |
| 6 | ~88% of opener | 1 | **Final warm-up single. Should feel fast and easy. This is the last set.** |

*Rest approximately 2–3 minutes between the lighter sets and 3–4 minutes before the final single.*

After the final warm-up single, she should feel warm, activated, and ready — not fatigued. If the final single felt heavy, do not add another set. Do not go heavier. Adrenaline on the platform will add perceived strength that is not present in the warm-up room. Trust the number.

**Between the final warm-up single and the opener:** keep moving lightly. Walk around, do a few bodyweight squats, stay warm. Do not sit down and go cold. Do not stand still and tighten up. Keep the body gently active.

---

### ~8:55 AM — Squat Opener
### *(first attempt on the platform)*

Walk out with the same setup she has rehearsed hundreds of times. The commands are the same as in training. The lift is the same as in training. The only thing that is different is the platform, the lights, and the crowd — and none of those things affect how strong she is.

**Cue hierarchy for the opener — keep it to two cues maximum.**
She should have identified her two most reliable, most automatic cues during the mock meet in Week 2. These are the only things she thinks about. Everything else is already in the body.

The opener should feel like a training lift. It should not be a grind. If it is a grind, the opener was too heavy and the second attempt needs to be adjusted immediately — this is a conversation you have with her the moment she racks the bar, not after she has already submitted the second attempt.

**White lights. Rack. Breathe. Next lift.**

---

### Between Squat Attempts

Submit the second attempt immediately after the opener — you have 60 seconds from when the bar is racked. Have the number ready before she walks onto the platform.

Between the first and second squat attempts, and between the second and third:
- Sit or stand comfortably — do not pace excessively
- Sip water
- Eat a small fast carbohydrate if the gap is long — a few gummy sweets, a rice cake, a banana
- One or two light bodyweight squats to stay loose, nothing more
- Review the cues for the next attempt briefly and then stop thinking about it

---

### Between Squat and Bench

The gap between the final squat attempt and the first bench attempt varies by meet format and flight size but is typically 20–40 minutes. Use this time deliberately.

**Immediately after the final squat:** sit down, remove knee sleeves, drink water, eat something. A banana, rice cakes, a small sandwich, gummy sweets — fast carbohydrates with a small amount of protein. The body has been working and glycogen is being used. Refuel now rather than waiting until you feel depleted.

**10–15 minutes before bench warm-up begins:** begin the bench-specific general warm-up.
- Band pull-aparts, 2 × 15
- Shoulder circles
- Light rotator cuff activation with a band — external rotation, face pulls
- A few press-up variations to activate the chest and triceps

**Bench warm-up sequence:**

| Set | Load | Reps | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Empty bar | 5 | Full setup — grip, arch, leg drive, pause. |
| 2 | ~45% of opener | 3 | |
| 3 | ~60% of opener | 2 | |
| 4 | ~73% of opener | 1 | Wrist wraps on. |
| 5 | ~85% of opener | 1 | **Final warm-up single.** |

The bench warm-up is shorter than the squat warm-up because the upper body recovers faster and requires less ramp-up time. The final single should be completed 5–6 minutes before the opener.

---

### Between Bench and Deadlift

Same protocol as between squat and bench. Eat, hydrate, rest briefly, then begin the deadlift-specific warm-up when the timing dictates.

**Deadlift warm-up sequence:**

| Set | Load | Reps | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ~40% of opener | 3 | Hip hinge focus. Full setup ritual. |
| 2 | ~55% of opener | 2 | |
| 3 | ~68% of opener | 2 | Belt on. |
| 4 | ~80% of opener | 1 | |
| 5 | ~87% of opener | 1 | **Final warm-up single.** |

One important note on the deadlift warm-up specifically: **keep it shorter than you think you need to.** By the time deadlifts begin, the body has already been through two full events and is physiologically primed. The deadlift warm-up does not need to be as extensive as the squat warm-up. Over-warming up for deadlifts is a common mistake that leaves athletes fatigued before their heaviest pulls of the day.

---

---

## Attempt Selection Decision Tree

This is the framework for making real-time attempt decisions on the day. Have this conversation with the client before the meet so she understands the logic and trusts the process when the adrenaline is running.

**After the opener:**

| How it felt | Decision |
|---|---|
| RPE 6–7, fast, easy | Proceed to planned second attempt as programmed |
| RPE 7–8, solid but worked for it | Proceed to planned second attempt or reduce by 2.5 kg |
| RPE 8–9, genuine grind but white lights | Reduce second attempt by 5 kg — protect the total |
| Red lights / missed lift | Repeat the opener on the second attempt — get the white lights |

**After the second attempt:**

| How it felt | Decision |
|---|---|
| RPE 7–8, moved well | Proceed to planned third attempt |
| RPE 8–9, hard but successful | Reduce third attempt by 2.5–5 kg or take a conservative PR |
| Missed lift | Assess whether a repeat is strategic or whether a small reduction gives a better chance of white lights |

**The governing rule for all attempt selection:** a successful lift at a lower weight is always better than a failed lift at a higher weight. Total is built on made attempts. Three white lights on the opener is worth more psychologically and strategically than a red-light second attempt at a number that looked impressive on paper.

---

---

## Psychological Framework for the Day

This section is for you as much as for her. How you communicate on meet day matters enormously.

**Before each lift — one or two cues only.** Not a technical lecture. Not a reminder of everything she has worked on. One cue, delivered calmly and with certainty. Then step back and let her lift.

**After a good lift — brief and positive.** "That was exactly right. Next one." Do not over-celebrate between attempts in a way that spikes adrenaline prematurely. Save the celebration for after the final deadlift.

**After a missed lift — calm, factual, forward-looking.** "Here is what happened. Here is what we do next. You have this." Do not dwell. Do not analyse in depth between attempts. The full debrief happens after the meet, over food, when the adrenaline has cleared.

**If she is in her head — redirect to the physical.** Anxiety lives in the abstract. Bring her back to something concrete and sensory: the feeling of the bar in her hands, the pressure of her feet on the floor, the breath before the unrack. The body knows what to do. The mind just needs to get out of the way.

**The most important thing you can communicate all day, in words or simply in your demeanour:** *you have already done the work. Today is just the demonstration.*

# Inserting a Deload Week
### Revised Block Structure: Now 4 Weeks to Meet

---

## First — An Honest Assessment

Before building the deload, it is worth pausing on what "rough accumulation block" means in practice, because the answer changes the deload prescription meaningfully. A rough block can mean several different things and they are not all treated the same way.

**If rough means high fatigue — she trained hard, volume was significant, she is beaten up physically but healthy.** This is the most common scenario and the most straightforward to address. A standard deload with reduced volume and maintained intensity will clear the fatigue and she will come out the other side feeling significantly better within 5–7 days. This is a good problem to have — it means the accumulation block did its job.

**If rough means disrupted — missed sessions, inconsistent training, life got in the way.** This is a different situation. The fatigue load may actually be lower than expected, but so is the fitness stimulus. In this case the deload needs to be lighter and shorter, and Week 1 of the peak may need to carry slightly more volume than originally programmed to compensate for the lost accumulation stimulus.

**If rough means a minor injury or persistent pain is present.** This needs to be addressed directly and honestly before any programming decision is made. A deload will not fix a structural problem — it will simply delay the conversation. If there is genuine pain on any of the competition lifts, that information changes everything about how the next four weeks are managed.

**Ask your client directly which of these applies** before implementing the programme below. The framework that follows assumes the first scenario — high fatigue from a demanding but complete accumulation block — as this is the most likely situation and the one where a deload is most clearly indicated and most clearly beneficial.

---

## Revised Block Overview

The meet is now 28 days away. The structure becomes four distinct phases, each with a clear physiological purpose.

| Week | Theme | Distance from Meet | Volume | Top Intensity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Week 1 | Deload | 28–22 days out | ~30–35% of final accum. week | 75–80% |
| Week 2 | Controlled Reduction | 21–15 days out | ~60% of final accum. week | 82–85% |
| Week 3 | Peak Intensity | 14–8 days out | ~40% of final accum. week | 92–93% |
| Week 4 | Taper | 7–0 days out | ~20% of final accum. week | 78–82% |

The original Weeks 1, 2, and 3 of the peak block remain structurally intact and simply shift forward by one week. Nothing about them changes. What is inserted before them is a genuine deload — not a light training week, not a reduced accumulation week, but a deliberate and aggressive offloading of both volume and intensity designed to clear fatigue as efficiently as possible.

---

---

# WEEK 1 — Deload
### Theme: *Clear the fatigue. Protect the pattern. Do not train hard.*

The word deload is used loosely in most gym settings to mean a slightly easier week. That is not what this is. A true deload in the context of a fatigued athlete four weeks from a powerlifting meet is an aggressive reduction in training stress — volume drops to roughly a third of the final accumulation week, intensity stays moderate rather than high, and the athlete leaves every session feeling better than when she arrived. If she finishes any session this week feeling worked, something has gone wrong.

The competition lifts are still performed every session. Movement pattern continuity matters — you do not want her to walk into Week 2 feeling like the squat is unfamiliar. But the loading is conservative, the rep ranges are low, and the total number of sets is minimal. Think of this week as maintenance of the pattern, not stimulus for adaptation.

**Training frequency: 3 days.** Down from 4 in the original Week 1. The extra rest day is not wasted — it is doing exactly what it needs to do.

---

### Day 1 — Squat and Deadlift

**Warm-up:** Full general warm-up as normal — do not abbreviate the warm-up just because the session is light. The warm-up serves a different purpose than the working sets and should remain thorough.

**Competition Squat**
- 1 × 5 @ 60%
- 1 × 3 @ 70%
- 2 × 2 @ 75%

*Four total working sets. The 75% doubles should feel almost trivially easy — if they do not, the accumulation block was even more taxing than anticipated and you may want to keep intensity here for an extra day before progressing. Bar speed is the metric that matters this week more than any percentage. Every rep should move fast.*

**Competition Deadlift**
- 1 × 3 @ 60%
- 2 × 2 @ 70%

*Three sets only. Pull from the floor with full setup ritual — stance, grip, brace, pull — but do not chase intensity. The deadlift is the most systemically taxing of the three lifts and gets the most conservative treatment this week.*

**No accessory work on this day.** The session ends after the deadlift sets. Total time including warm-up should be 45–55 minutes. If it feels too short, that is correct.

---

### Day 2 — Bench Press

**Warm-up:** Band pull-aparts, shoulder circles, rotator cuff activation, empty bar work.

**Competition Bench Press**
- 1 × 5 @ 60%
- 1 × 3 @ 70%
- 2 × 3 @ 75%

*The bench recovers faster than the squat and deadlift and tolerates slightly higher rep counts at this intensity without meaningful fatigue cost. Three reps at 75% rather than doubles — still well within the deload parameters.*

**Dumbbell Row**
- 2 × 8 per side @ RPE 5
*Upper back health. Keep it genuinely easy.*

**Face Pulls**
- 2 × 15 with light band or cable

*That is the entire session. Upper body accessory work is kept to two movements and both are health-maintenance rather than strength stimulus. No tricep work, no overhead pressing, nothing that adds meaningful fatigue to the pressing pattern.*

---

### Day 3 — Full Body, Light

This session exists to maintain movement frequency across all three competition lifts without adding meaningful fatigue. It is the shortest session of the week and should feel almost like an extended warm-up.

**Competition Squat**
- 1 × 3 @ 65%
- 1 × 2 @ 72%

**Competition Bench Press**
- 1 × 3 @ 65%
- 1 × 2 @ 72%

**Competition Deadlift**
- 1 × 3 @ 62%
- 1 × 1 @ 70%

*Six working sets across three lifts. The session is over in 35–40 minutes including warm-up. This is intentional. The athlete should leave feeling loose, mobile, and slightly frustrated that she did not do more — that frustration is the deload working.*

---

### Deload Week Cardio

The cardio sessions from the original programme are retained this week but kept at the lower end of the prescribed durations. Fatigue clearance is the priority and easy aerobic work supports it.

**Rest Day 1 — Walk, 20 minutes.** Easy pace, outdoors if possible. No heart rate target — simply move and breathe.

**Rest Day 2 — Stationary bike, 15 minutes.** Low resistance, comfortable cadence. A metabolic flush rather than a cardiovascular session.

**Rest Day 3 — Walk, 15–20 minutes.** Same as Rest Day 1. This is the final rest day before Week 2 begins — keep it easy and use the walk to mentally transition into the peak block mindset.

No post-session bike flushes this week — the sessions are short enough that they do not generate the metabolic byproduct accumulation that makes the flush valuable.

---

### Deload Week Nutrition

This is where many athletes make a mistake. The instinct when training volume drops is to reduce calories proportionally — less work, less food. Resist this entirely. Caloric intake should remain at or above maintenance throughout the deload week for two reasons.

First, the body is actively repairing tissue and consolidating the adaptations from the accumulation block. This process requires energy and protein. Cutting calories during a deload is nutritionally equivalent to doing renovation work on a house and then turning off the electricity — the materials are there but the tools do not work.

Second, glycogen stores need to be fully replenished after a demanding accumulation block. This takes several days of adequate carbohydrate intake and cannot be rushed by eating more in a single day. Consistent moderate-to-high carbohydrate intake across the full deload week is the correct approach.

**Protein remains at 1.8–2.2 g per kg of bodyweight.** Carbohydrates remain moderate to high. Fat at normal levels. Total calories at maintenance or slightly above. This is not a body composition week — it is a recovery week, and recovery requires fuel.

If the client is managing weight for a weight class, this week is still not the time for restriction. Monitor morning weight daily, note the trend, and plan any necessary adjustments for later in the block. Aggressive restriction during a deload actively undermines the recovery process the deload is designed to create.

---

### Deload Week Recovery Notes

Sleep becomes even more important this week than in a normal training week because the primary adaptation stimulus is now recovery rather than training. The body does its repair work during sleep and the deload week is essentially a concentrated repair window. **Target 8–9 hours every night, with consistent sleep and wake times.** Irregular sleep schedules — even with adequate total hours — disrupt the hormonal environment that governs recovery.

Soft tissue work is actively encouraged this week in a way it is not during heavier training weeks. A sports massage, if accessible and affordable, is an excellent investment during the deload — ideally on Day 2 or Day 3 of the week when the initial acute soreness from the first session has cleared. Foam rolling and massage gun work on the quads, hamstrings, glutes, thoracic spine, and lats for 10–15 minutes daily is beneficial and costs nothing.

Stress management outside the gym matters this week. A rough accumulation block often correlates with a rough life period — work stress, poor sleep, disrupted routine. If any of those external stressors are still present, address them directly where possible. The deload week is a good time to have that conversation with the client about what is going on outside the gym, because the external environment is now the primary variable affecting recovery rate.

---

### What to Watch For During the Deload

Two things can go wrong during a deload week and both are worth monitoring.

**The client trains too hard.** This is by far the more common problem. She feels good on Day 1, the bar moves fast, and the instinct is to add sets or push the intensity. Do not allow this. The bar feels fast precisely because the loads are conservative — that is the point. Adding sets because things feel good is the equivalent of spending savings because the bank account looks healthy. The deload is an investment in meet day, not an invitation to train.

**The client feels worse, not better, mid-week.** This is also normal and worth flagging in advance so it does not cause alarm. Days 3 and 4 of a deload week often feel flat, heavy, and psychologically low. This is sometimes called the **deload dip** — fatigue is clearing but the fitness expression that comes with full recovery has not yet arrived. It typically resolves by Days 5–7. If the client messages you on Wednesday of the deload week saying she feels terrible and weak, the correct response is: this is exactly what is supposed to happen, keep eating, keep sleeping, and trust the process.

---

## A Note on the Revised Timeline

Adding this deload week does not compromise the peak block — it strengthens it. The original three-week peak assumed a client arriving at Week 1 with manageable fatigue. If the accumulation block was genuinely rough, that assumption was incorrect, and programming a peak on top of unresolved fatigue produces a suboptimal result. The deload corrects the starting conditions so that the peak block can do what it was designed to do.

She now arrives at the original Week 1 — now Week 2 of the revised block — with cleared fatigue, full glycogen, and a nervous system that is ready to respond to the intensity ramp. The mock meet in Week 3 will be more representative of her true capability. The taper in Week 4 will land on a body that is genuinely ready to express its fitness rather than one that is still carrying the residue of a difficult training cycle.

Four weeks is a better runway than three for an athlete in this condition. The meet date has not changed. The outcome is now more likely to reflect what she actually built over the preceding twelve weeks.

That is the whole point.

# 95% Singles in Week 2
### Opener Confirmation Protocol

---

## Before Adding the Sets — A Direct Conversation

This is a reasonable request and a common instinct among competitive lifters. Touching near-opener weight before the meet feels like confirmation, like proof that the number is real. That instinct is not wrong — there is genuine value in a heavy single during a peak block, and the original programme already included opener simulation work at 92–93% in Week 2 for exactly this reason.

But 95% sits in a specific and somewhat uncomfortable place in the peaking context, and before adding it to the programme you need to have an honest conversation with your client about what she is actually asking for and why.

**95% of training max is not the opener. It is between the opener and the second attempt.** If her opener is at 90–92% and her second attempt is at 97–100%, a 95% single in training is heavier than her planned opener and approaching her planned second. That is meaningful. It means the fatigue cost is real, the injury risk is non-trivial compared to an 88% single, and the psychological information it provides — while valuable — comes at a price that needs to be consciously accepted.

The question to ask her is this: **what specifically are you trying to confirm?**

If the answer is *"I want to know the opener is there"* — the 92–93% single already in the programme answers that question with lower risk.

If the answer is *"I want to know my second attempt is realistic"* — a 95% single is a reasonable way to gather that information, provided it is programmed carefully and the recovery cost is accounted for.

If the answer is *"I just need to feel a heavy bar before the meet or I won't feel ready"* — that is a psychological need, not a physiological one, and it is completely valid. Acknowledge it as such and programme accordingly, but make sure she understands the trade-off she is accepting.

Assuming she understands the above and still wants the 95% singles — and this is a legitimate choice — here is how to do it as safely and intelligently as possible.

---

## Programming Principles for the 95% Singles

Three rules govern how these singles are inserted.

**Rule one: Not all three lifts on the same day.** Testing a 95% squat, bench, and deadlift in a single session is a mock meet at near-maximal intensity. That is not a peaking tool — that is a competition, and it will generate a fatigue debt that the taper week cannot fully clear in time. The three singles are distributed across two sessions with adequate recovery between them.

**Rule two: Deadlift gets the most conservative treatment.** The deadlift has the longest recovery demand of the three lifts. A 95% deadlift single generates significantly more systemic fatigue than a 95% squat or bench single. It is programmed last in the week, on its own day, with nothing else of consequence around it.

**Rule three: If a single looks or feels wrong, it stops there.** Establish this with the client in advance. If the squat single at 95% is a genuine grind — RPE 9 or above, form breakdown, significant struggle — the bench and deadlift singles are reduced to 90–92% or removed entirely. One bad single is information. Pushing through three bad singles is how people get hurt three weeks before a meet.

---

## Revised Week 2 Structure

Week 2 now runs across **four days** rather than three to distribute the heavy singles appropriately. The original three-day structure compressed too much intensity into too little space once 95% singles are added. The extra day costs one additional day of fatigue but provides significantly better recovery between the heavy efforts.

---

### Day 1 — Squat 95% Single + Bench Moderate
### *(Monday or Tuesday)*

**Warm-up:** Full general warm-up — 10 minutes. Leg swings, hip circles, goblet squat, thoracic rotation. Do not abbreviate this warm-up. The nervous system needs time to arrive before a near-maximal effort.

**Competition Squat — Opener Confirmation Single**

Work up deliberately. The jumps between sets should be comfortable and the bar should feel faster with each warm-up set as the nervous system activates. If the bar is slowing down during the warm-up rather than speeding up, that is a signal worth noting.

- 1 × 5 @ 50%
- 1 × 3 @ 60%
- 1 × 2 @ 70%
- 1 × 1 @ 80%
- 1 × 1 @ 87%
- 1 × 1 @ 92%
- **1 × 1 @ 95% ← The confirmation single**

*Rest 4–5 minutes before the 92% single. Rest a full 5 minutes before the 95% single. Do not rush this. The warm-up sets are not the workout — they are preparation for the one set that matters.*

**What you are looking for at 95%:** The lift should be hard but not a grind. RPE 8 to 8.5 is the target — one to one and a half reps left in the tank, technically sound, no significant form breakdown. If it moves at RPE 8 or below, the opener is confirmed and the second attempt can be set with confidence. If it moves at RPE 9, the opener is still likely fine but the second attempt should be conservative. If it is a true RPE 9.5 or above — a real fight — have the conversation about whether the opener needs to come down.

**After the squat single — rest 8–10 minutes before touching the bench bar.** This is longer than a normal inter-exercise rest and it is intentional. The squat single has taxed the entire system and the bench needs to be performed with a nervous system that has partially recovered, not one that is still processing a near-maximal squat.

**Competition Bench Press — Moderate Work**

This is not a heavy bench day. The squat single has already generated significant fatigue and the bench single is coming on Day 2. Today's bench work is moderate intensity maintenance — keeping the pattern fresh without adding meaningful fatigue.

- 1 × 3 @ 70%
- 1 × 2 @ 78%
- 1 × 1 @ 83%

*Three sets. The 83% single should feel comfortable — RPE 7 at most. If it feels heavier than that, drop it to 80% and make a note. The body is telling you something about its current recovery state.*

**Session ends here.** No accessory work. No additional sets. Total session time 75–90 minutes including warm-up.

---

### Day 2 — Bench 95% Single
### *(Wednesday — at least 48 hours after Day 1)*

The bench gets its own dedicated day. Upper body recovers faster than lower body and the bench single will not generate the same systemic fatigue as the squat single, but giving it a dedicated session means it can be approached fresh and treated with the same seriousness as the squat single received on Day 1.

**Warm-up:** Band pull-aparts 2 × 15, shoulder circles, rotator cuff activation, floor press with empty bar. 8–10 minutes total.

**Competition Bench Press — Opener Confirmation Single**

- 1 × 5 @ 50%
- 1 × 3 @ 62%
- 1 × 2 @ 72%
- 1 × 1 @ 80%
- 1 × 1 @ 87%
- 1 × 1 @ 92%
- **1 × 1 @ 95% ← The confirmation single**

*Rest 3–4 minutes between the lighter sets. Rest a full 4–5 minutes before the 92% and 95% singles. Every rep from the 80% single onwards is performed to full competition standard — pause on the chest, wait for the press command, full lockout, wait for the rack command. No touch-and-go, no abbreviated pauses. If she cannot white-light it in the warm-up room she cannot white-light it on the platform.*

**What you are looking for at 95%:** Same RPE framework as the squat — target RPE 8 to 8.5. Pay particular attention to the pause and the press command on this single. Meet nerves sometimes cause lifters to jump the press command in competition, and a heavy single in training is a good opportunity to reinforce the habit of waiting. If the pause feels long and uncomfortable at 95%, that is normal and will feel shorter on the platform with adrenaline running.

**After the bench single:**

**Close-Grip Bench Press**
- 2 × 3 @ 65%

*The only accessory work this session. Tricep reinforcement without meaningful fatigue addition. Keep it crisp and technical.*

**Face Pulls**
- 2 × 15

Session ends. 50–65 minutes total.

---

### Day 3 — Deadlift 95% Single
### *(Friday — at least 48 hours after Day 2)*

The deadlift single gets the most space of the three. It is programmed at the end of the week, after the squat and bench singles have been completed and partially recovered from, and it stands alone with nothing else of consequence in the session. The deadlift is the lift that most commonly causes problems when pushed too hard too close to a meet — lower back fatigue, grip fatigue, and general systemic stress all accumulate here in a way they do not with the other two lifts.

**Warm-up:** Hip hinge patterning — kettlebell deadlift × 10, band-resisted hip extension × 10, hamstring stretch. 8 minutes.

**Competition Deadlift — Opener Confirmation Single**

- 1 × 3 @ 50%
- 1 × 2 @ 62%
- 1 × 1 @ 72%
- 1 × 1 @ 80%
- 1 × 1 @ 87%
- 1 × 1 @ 92%
- **1 × 1 @ 95% ← The confirmation single**

*Rest 4–5 minutes before the 87% single. Rest a full 5–6 minutes before the 92% single. Rest a full 6 minutes before the 95% single. The deadlift warm-up rests are longer than the squat and bench rests because the posterior chain and lower back need more time between near-maximal efforts.*

**What you are looking for at 95%:** In addition to the RPE framework, watch specifically for lower back rounding, grip failure, and hip rise off the floor. A 95% deadlift that is technically sound at RPE 8 is excellent information. A 95% deadlift that is technically compromised — even if it locks out — is a warning sign that either the opener needs adjusting or that the accumulation block left more fatigue in the posterior chain than anticipated.

**After the deadlift single — the session is over.** No accessory work. No additional pulling. No leg work. Walk out of the gym.

Total session time: 55–70 minutes including warm-up.

---

### Day 4 — Mock Meet Simulation
### *(Saturday or Sunday — 24–48 hours after Day 3)*

The original mock meet session from the peak block is retained but the intensities are adjusted downward. The client has just completed three near-maximal singles across three days — the mock meet is not the place to push intensity again. Its purpose this week is movement rehearsal, psychological preparation, and meet-day logistics practice. The weights are deliberately conservative.

**Squat**
- Work up to 1 × 1 @ 82%
- 1 × 1 @ 87%

**Bench Press**
- Work up to 1 × 1 @ 82%
- 1 × 1 @ 87%

**Deadlift**
- Work up to 1 × 1 @ 80%
- 1 × 1 @ 85%

*Everything at competition standard. Full equipment. Full commands. The bar should feel fast and the session should feel easy. If anything feels heavy at these percentages after the week of heavy singles, that is the accumulated fatigue of the week expressing itself — it will clear during the taper. Do not add sets.*

**Post-session debrief:** This is the most important coaching conversation of the entire block. Review all three confirmation singles. Confirm openers. Set second attempts. Discuss what the 95% singles told you about where she actually is versus where the training max suggested she was. Adjust the meet attempt card accordingly.

---

## Revised Full Block Overview

| Week | Theme | Sessions | Top Intensity | Key Feature |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Week 1 | Deload | 3 | 75% | Fatigue clearance |
| Week 2 | Controlled Reduction | 4 | 85% | Volume reduction, pattern maintenance |
| Week 3 | Peak Intensity + 95% Singles | 4 | 95% | Opener confirmation, mock meet |
| Week 4 | Taper | 2 | 78–82% | Full recovery, meet preparation |
| Meet Day | Compete | — | 100%+ | — |

---

## What the 95% Singles Actually Tell You

A single data point from a heavy training single is useful but not definitive. Here is how to interpret what you see across all three lifts and what decisions it should drive.

**If all three singles move at RPE 8 or below:** The training max is accurate or slightly conservative. Openers are confirmed. Second attempts can be set at the upper end of the planned range. Consider whether the third attempts are appropriately ambitious.

**If all three singles move at RPE 8.5–9:** The training max is accurate. Openers are confirmed but should not be increased. Second attempts stay at the planned numbers. Third attempts should be realistic rather than aspirational.

**If one lift moves significantly harder than the others:** That lift's opener may need a small reduction — 2.5 to 5 kg. The other two lifts proceed as planned. This is useful information that would not have been available without the singles.

**If any single is a genuine RPE 9.5 or above, or is missed:** Do not panic. Do not add extra sessions. Do not attempt to retest. Reduce the opener for that lift by 5 kg, accept the information, and trust that the taper will restore more than it appears. A hard single in training three weeks out does not predict a hard opener on meet day — the taper, the adrenaline, and the full recovery between now and then change the equation significantly.

---

## The Risk Register

Adding 95% singles to a peaking block is a legitimate programming choice and this plan manages the risk as carefully as possible. But the risks are real and your client should know them explicitly.

**Injury risk is elevated compared to 88–92% work.** Not dramatically, but meaningfully. The difference between a training single at 92% and one at 95% is small in percentage terms and significant in absolute load. Ensure the warm-up is thorough, the technique is sound on every warm-up set, and there is no ego involved in the execution. If anything feels wrong during the warm-up — a tweak, unusual tightness, a joint that is not tracking correctly — the single does not happen that day.

**Fatigue cost extends into Week 4.** Three singles at 95% across three days will leave a residue that the taper week needs to clear. This is manageable — the taper is designed to handle it — but it means the early days of Week 4 may feel heavier than the original programme intended. Reassure the client that this is expected and does not require any modification to the taper sessions.

**The psychological risk cuts both ways.** A successful 95% single builds enormous confidence. A difficult one can plant doubt that is hard to uproot in the days before a meet. Prepare the client for both outcomes in advance so that neither one catches her off guard. The singles are information — they are not verdicts.

# Pre-Meet Nutrition Protocol
### The 48 Hours Before the Platform

---

## The Governing Principle

The 48 hours before a powerlifting meet is not the time to build anything. Muscle is not synthesised in 48 hours. Strength is not gained. The entire nutritional focus of this window is a single objective: **place the body in the most favourable physiological state possible to express the strength that already exists.** That means full glycogen stores, optimal hydration, stable blood sugar, a comfortable and functional digestive system, and a bodyweight that is where it needs to be for weigh-in without any last-minute panic.

Everything in this protocol is in service of those outcomes. Nothing else matters nutritionally in this window.

One important framing note before the specifics: **this protocol assumes a same-day weigh-in or a weigh-in the morning of the meet.** If the federation uses a 24-hour weigh-in — where athletes weigh in the day before and have a full night to rehydrate and refuel — the protocol is somewhat different and more aggressive refeeding is both possible and appropriate. Confirm the weigh-in format with your client and adjust accordingly. The framework below is written for the more common and more demanding same-day or morning-of scenario.

---

---

## The Weight Class Situation — Address This First

Before discussing carbohydrates and sodium, the weight class question needs to be resolved because it determines everything else about how these 48 hours are managed.

**Scenario A — She is comfortably within her weight class with no meaningful cut required.**

This is the ideal situation and the one this protocol is primarily written for. If she is within 1–2 kg of the weight class limit at her normal walking weight, the 48 hours before the meet is straightforward nutrition optimisation with no restriction component. Follow the full protocol below without modification.

**Scenario B — She needs to drop 2–4 kg for weigh-in.**

This is manageable but requires careful planning and should not be left to the 48-hour window to solve. A cut of this magnitude in 48 hours relies primarily on water and food volume manipulation — reducing sodium in the days prior to cause water release, reducing fibre and food volume to clear the gut, and potentially a small amount of active sweating if necessary. The refeed after weigh-in then becomes critically important. If this is her situation, the sodium and fluid sections below become even more important and the carbohydrate loading needs to be timed carefully around the weigh-in rather than simply across the full 48 hours.

**Scenario C — She needs to drop more than 4 kg.**

This is outside the scope of a training programme document and requires direct involvement from a sports dietitian. Aggressive water cuts in the 48 hours before a meet carry genuine health risks and significantly impair performance if the refeed is insufficient. If this is the situation, have that conversation now — not in the final week.

The protocol below assumes Scenario A or the lighter end of Scenario B.

---

---

# 48 HOURS OUT
## Two Days Before the Meet — The Foundation Day

This day is about building the glycogen stores that will fuel the meet. It is not a dramatic carbohydrate loading day in the classic endurance sports sense — powerlifting does not deplete glycogen the way a marathon does — but full glycogen stores contribute meaningfully to strength output, psychological sharpness, and the physical feeling of being ready. An athlete who arrives at a meet with partially depleted glycogen feels flat, heavy, and weak even if her actual strength capacity is unchanged. The perception matters.

---

### Total Caloric Target

**Maintenance calories or 10–15% above.** This is not a surplus large enough to cause meaningful water retention or digestive discomfort, but it is enough to ensure glycogen stores are being topped up rather than merely maintained. For most intermediate female lifters this means somewhere in the range of 2,000–2,600 kcal depending on bodyweight and individual metabolism. Use her established maintenance number as the anchor.

---

### Carbohydrates — The Priority Macronutrient Today

**Target: 5–7 grams of carbohydrate per kilogram of bodyweight.**

For a 70 kg athlete this means 350–490 grams of carbohydrate across the day. This sounds like a large number and it is — but spread across three meals and two snacks it is entirely achievable without discomfort.

**Carbohydrate sources to prioritise:**
White rice, pasta, bread, potatoes, oats, rice cakes, bananas, fruit juice, sports drinks, honey, jam, bagels. These are all easily digestible, low-fibre, and well-tolerated by most athletes. The emphasis on white rather than wholegrain versions is deliberate — lower fibre means faster digestion, less gut bulk, and less likelihood of gastrointestinal discomfort during the meet.

**Carbohydrate sources to avoid today:**
High-fibre vegetables in large quantities, legumes, beans, lentils, bran cereals, wholegrain products in large amounts, cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, cauliflower, and cabbage. These are excellent foods in normal life and terrible choices in the 48 hours before a powerlifting meet. They ferment in the gut, produce gas, and create the kind of digestive discomfort that is distracting at best and genuinely problematic at worst when you are braced maximally under a heavy squat.

**Sample carbohydrate distribution across the day:**
- Breakfast: Oats with banana and honey — approximately 80–100 g carbohydrate
- Mid-morning snack: Rice cakes with jam — approximately 40–50 g carbohydrate
- Lunch: Large portion of white rice or pasta with a moderate protein source — approximately 120–150 g carbohydrate
- Afternoon snack: Banana and a sports drink or fruit juice — approximately 50–60 g carbohydrate
- Dinner: Pasta or rice with protein, bread on the side — approximately 120–150 g carbohydrate

Total across the day: approximately 410–510 g. Adjust portions up or down based on her bodyweight and individual tolerance.

---

### Protein — Maintain, Do Not Overload

**Target: 1.6–2.0 grams per kilogram of bodyweight.** Slightly lower than the training week target because the priority today is carbohydrates and excess protein competes for digestive capacity and caloric space. Protein sources should be lean and easily digestible — chicken breast, white fish, eggs, Greek yoghurt, protein shakes if needed to hit the target without adding significant fat or fibre.

Avoid very high-fat protein sources today — fatty cuts of red meat, full-fat dairy in large quantities, fried proteins. Fat slows gastric emptying and a meal that is still sitting heavily in the stomach the morning of the meet is a problem that begins here.

---

### Fat — Moderate and Functional

**Target: 0.8–1.0 grams per kilogram of bodyweight.** Fat is not the enemy today but it is not the priority either. Keep it at normal levels — enough to support hormone function, fat-soluble vitamin absorption, and satiety, but not so high that it slows digestion or competes with carbohydrate for caloric space. A small amount of olive oil in cooking, a tablespoon of peanut butter on rice cakes, a handful of nuts as part of a snack — these are all fine. A large creamy pasta dish, a meal heavy in cheese, or a high-fat takeaway are not.

---

### Sodium — The Strategic Variable

Sodium management in the 48 hours before a meet is one of the most misunderstood areas of competition nutrition. The instinct among many athletes is to restrict sodium aggressively in the days before the meet to reduce water retention and make weight. This instinct is frequently counterproductive and sometimes actively harmful.

**Here is the physiology:** sodium is the primary extracellular electrolyte and it governs fluid distribution throughout the body. Adequate sodium intake supports plasma volume, which supports cardiovascular function, which supports the delivery of oxygen and nutrients to working muscles. An athlete who has aggressively restricted sodium for several days arrives at the meet with reduced plasma volume, impaired thermoregulation, and a tendency toward cramping — none of which are conducive to a good total.

**The correct approach depends on the weight situation.**

**If she is comfortably within her weight class:** Keep sodium at normal dietary levels today — approximately 2,000–3,000 mg, which is roughly what a normal diet without excessive processed food provides. Do not add extra sodium and do not restrict it. Normal is correct.

**If she needs to drop 1–2 kg for weigh-in:** A moderate sodium reduction today — dropping to approximately 1,500–2,000 mg — will cause a small amount of water release over the following 24 hours without meaningfully impairing performance. This is achieved simply by avoiding added salt, processed foods, cured meats, soy sauce, and restaurant meals. Cook at home with minimal added salt. This is a gentle manipulation, not an aggressive cut.

**If she needs to drop 2–4 kg:** Sodium restriction today drops to approximately 1,000–1,500 mg and is combined with a moderate reduction in food volume and fibre to clear gut weight. This is the upper limit of what should be attempted without professional dietary supervision. After weigh-in, sodium is reintroduced aggressively as part of the refeed — more on this below.

**Foods to avoid for sodium reduction if needed:**
Processed meats, canned foods, cheese, bread in large quantities, restaurant and takeaway food, sauces and condiments, sports drinks with high sodium content, salted nuts.

---

### Fluids — Begin Building Hydration Today

**Target: 3–4 litres of water across the day.** This is above normal daily intake for most people and is intentional. The goal is to arrive at the meet in a state of optimal hydration — not overhydrated, which causes its own problems, but fully hydrated with well-functioning kidneys and good plasma volume.

Spread fluid intake evenly across the day rather than front-loading or back-loading it. Drinking two litres in the evening to hit a target is not the same as drinking consistently throughout the day and does not produce the same hydration state.

**Fluid sources:**
Water is the primary vehicle. Diluted fruit juice, herbal tea, and coconut water are all acceptable secondary sources. Avoid alcohol entirely — it is a diuretic, it disrupts sleep, and it impairs recovery. Avoid excessive caffeine in the afternoon and evening — it disrupts sleep and has a mild diuretic effect at high doses.

**Urine colour is the practical monitoring tool.** Target pale yellow — the colour of lemonade — throughout the day. Dark yellow or amber means drink more. Completely clear means she has overshot and can ease off slightly.

---

### The 48-Hour Dinner — The Most Important Meal of This Window

Dinner two nights before the meet deserves specific attention because it is the meal that most directly loads glycogen for the following day's competition. It should be the largest carbohydrate meal of the day, eaten at a comfortable time — not so late that digestion is still active at bedtime.

**The ideal dinner:**
A large portion of white pasta or rice — 150–200 grams dry weight — with a lean protein source such as chicken breast or white fish, a small amount of easily digestible vegetables such as courgette, cucumber, or well-cooked carrots, and bread on the side if appetite allows. A small dessert of something sweet — ice cream, a banana with honey, a small portion of cake — is not only acceptable but actively useful for topping up glycogen.

This is not the night for a new restaurant, an experimental cuisine, or a meal that has not been eaten before. Familiar food, well-tolerated, eaten calmly and without rush.

---

# 24 HOURS OUT
## The Day Before the Meet — Consolidation and Fine-Tuning

This day has a different character from the day before. The heavy glycogen loading work is largely done — the body can only store a finite amount of glycogen and most of it was loaded yesterday. Today is about maintaining what has been built, managing bodyweight for weigh-in, keeping the digestive system calm, and arriving at bedtime feeling ready rather than stuffed, anxious, or depleted.

---

### Carbohydrates — Maintain, Do Not Overload

**Target: 4–5 grams per kilogram of bodyweight.** Slightly lower than yesterday because the glycogen stores are already well-stocked and excess carbohydrate today will simply be stored as fat or cause water retention rather than adding meaningfully to glycogen. The same food sources apply — white, easily digestible, low-fibre.

A common mistake on the day before a meet is eating an enormous amount of carbohydrate in a panic, having eaten normally for the preceding days. This causes bloating, digestive discomfort, disrupted sleep, and a feeling of heaviness on meet morning that is the opposite of what is wanted. The loading was yesterday. Today is maintenance.

---

### Protein — Keep It Consistent

**Target: 1.6–2.0 grams per kilogram of bodyweight.** Same as yesterday. Same lean, easily digestible sources. No change needed here.

---

### Fat — Keep It Low Today

**Target: 0.6–0.8 grams per kilogram of bodyweight.** Slightly lower than yesterday. Fat today is purely functional — enough to support normal physiological processes but not enough to slow digestion or add unnecessary caloric density. This is the day to avoid the high-fat meals most aggressively.

---

### Sodium — The Decision Point

Today's sodium strategy depends entirely on the weigh-in situation.

**If comfortably within weight class:** Normal sodium intake. No restriction, no loading. Approximately 2,000–2,500 mg across the day from normal food sources. Do not overthink this.

**If using mild sodium restriction for weight management:** Continue the moderate restriction from yesterday — approximately 1,500–2,000 mg. By this point the mild water release from reduced sodium will be expressing itself and morning weight should be tracking in the right direction.

**If a same-day weigh-in and she is within 1–2 kg:** The morning of the meet she will weigh in, and then the refeed begins immediately. In this case today's sodium can be kept low — 1,000–1,500 mg — to maximise the water release overnight, with the understanding that sodium is reintroduced aggressively after weigh-in as part of the refeed protocol.

**One important note on sodium and cramping:** if she has a history of cramping during competition, do not restrict sodium aggressively regardless of the weight situation. The cramping risk from low sodium in a high-stress, high-exertion environment outweighs the benefit of the small amount of water weight released. In this case keep sodium at normal levels and manage weight through food volume and fibre reduction only.

---

### Fluids — Taper Slightly if Making Weight, Maintain if Not

**If comfortably within weight class:** Continue at 3–3.5 litres across the day. Taper fluid intake in the two hours before bed to avoid disrupted sleep from overnight bathroom trips.

**If managing weight for weigh-in:** Reduce fluid intake slightly today — 2–2.5 litres — and stop drinking fluids approximately 2 hours before bed. This is a mild fluid restriction, not a dehydration protocol. The goal is to arrive at weigh-in slightly under the limit, not to be meaningfully dehydrated. Meaningful dehydration — more than 2–3% of bodyweight — impairs strength output and cognitive function and is not a strategy that serves a same-day weigh-in athlete well.

---

### The Day-Before Meal Structure

**Breakfast:** Moderate carbohydrate, lean protein, low fat, low fibre. Oats, eggs, toast, fruit juice. Normal and familiar.

**Lunch:** The largest meal of the day. White rice or pasta, lean protein, small amount of easily digestible vegetables. This should be eaten by early afternoon — no later than 2:00 PM — to allow full digestion before the evening.

**Afternoon snack:** Light carbohydrate — rice cakes, a banana, a small amount of fruit. Keep it simple.

**Dinner — the critical meal:** This is the last significant meal before meet morning and it deserves careful thought. It should be moderate in size — not a feast, not a restriction. The goal is to go to bed feeling satisfied and comfortable, not stuffed and not hungry.

**The ideal day-before dinner:**
White pasta or rice — a normal portion, not an enormous one — with a lean protein source. A small amount of bread. A simple dessert if desired. Eaten at least 2–3 hours before bed. No alcohol. No new foods. No restaurant gambles.

The most important quality of this meal is familiarity. She should have eaten this exact meal, or something very close to it, before a heavy training session at some point in the accumulation block. The digestive system should recognise it completely.

---

### Sleep Nutrition

If she wakes in the night and is genuinely hungry — which sometimes happens the night before a meet due to elevated metabolism and anxiety — a small, simple snack is better than lying awake hungry. A banana, a few rice cakes, a small glass of fruit juice. Nothing that requires digestion effort. Nothing that will cause her to feel heavy in the morning.

---

# WEIGH-IN AND IMMEDIATE REFEED
## If Same-Day Weigh-In

If the weigh-in is same-day — typically 1–2 hours before the first attempt — the refeed window is short and the protocol needs to be aggressive and well-planned.

**Immediately after stepping off the scale:**

**Fluids first.** Begin rehydrating immediately. 500–750 ml of water or an electrolyte drink in the first 15–20 minutes. Do not chug — drink steadily. Rapid large fluid intake can cause nausea and gastrointestinal discomfort. An electrolyte drink with sodium, potassium, and magnesium is preferable to plain water here because it supports faster fluid absorption and begins restoring the electrolyte balance that any mild cut will have disrupted.

**Sodium — reintroduce now.** If sodium was restricted in the preceding 24–48 hours, this is the moment to bring it back. Salted rice cakes, pretzels, a small amount of salted nuts, a sports drink with sodium content — these all serve the dual purpose of providing fast carbohydrates and reintroducing sodium to support fluid retention and plasma volume restoration.

**Fast carbohydrates — begin immediately.** The refeed meal should begin within 15–20 minutes of weigh-in. White rice, white bread, bananas, rice cakes with honey, sports drinks, gummy sweets — fast-digesting carbohydrates that begin restoring glycogen without sitting heavily in the stomach. Target 60–80 grams of carbohydrate in this first refeed window.

**Protein — moderate and lean.** 25–35 grams of lean protein alongside the carbohydrates. Chicken, eggs, a protein shake. Not a large fatty meal — the digestive system needs to process this quickly.

**Continue eating and drinking in the 60–90 minutes between weigh-in and warm-up.** Small amounts every 20–30 minutes rather than one large meal. The goal is steady glycogen restoration and hydration, not a single large bolus that sits in the stomach during the squat warm-up.

**By the time the squat warm-up begins**, she should have consumed approximately 100–150 grams of carbohydrate and 500–1,000 ml of fluid since weigh-in. This is achievable in a 60–90 minute window and will meaningfully restore performance capacity compared to arriving at the warm-up room still depleted.

---

## The 48-Hour Nutrition Summary

| Timepoint | Carbs (g/kg) | Protein (g/kg) | Fat (g/kg) | Sodium | Fluids |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 48 hours out | 5–7 | 1.6–2.0 | 0.8–1.0 | Normal or mild restriction | 3–4 litres |
| 24 hours out | 4–5 | 1.6–2.0 | 0.6–0.8 | Normal or moderate restriction | 2.5–3.5 litres |
| Meet morning meal | 1.5–2.0 | 0.4–0.5 | Minimal | Normal | 500–750 ml with meal |
| Between flights | 0.5–1.0 per flight | Small amounts | Minimal | Normal to moderate | Sip consistently |
| Post weigh-in refeed | 1.5–2.0 in 90 min | 0.3–0.4 | Minimal | Reintroduce actively | 500–1000 ml in 90 min |

## The Things That Derail This Protocol

Document these explicitly with your client so she can avoid them.

**Eating a new food in the 48-hour window.** The night before a meet is not the time to try a new restaurant, a new cuisine, or a food she has not eaten before training. Gastrointestinal distress on the platform is entirely preventable and entirely devastating. Familiar food only.

**Undereating because nerves suppress appetite.** Pre-competition anxiety commonly reduces appetite. The client may not feel hungry the day before the meet and may be tempted to eat less than the protocol prescribes. Eating is not optional in this window — it is preparation. Encourage her to eat to the protocol regardless of appetite signals, using easily consumed foods like smoothies, fruit juice, and sports drinks if solid food feels unappealing.

**Overeating in a panic.** The opposite problem — eating an enormous amount of carbohydrate the night before because she suddenly worries she has not loaded enough. This causes bloating, disrupted sleep, and a heavy feeling on meet morning. The loading was built across both days. Trust the process.

**Alcohol.** It impairs sleep quality, is a diuretic, elevates cortisol, and impairs glycogen synthesis. Not a single drink in the 48-hour window. This is non-negotiable.

**Excessive caffeine late in the day.** A normal morning coffee is fine. Caffeine after 2:00 PM on the day before the meet risks disrupting sleep. Save the caffeine strategy for meet morning — a well-timed pre-meet caffeine dose of 3–6 mg per kilogram of bodyweight approximately 45–60 minutes before the first attempt is a legitimate and well-evidenced performance tool. But that is meet morning, not the night before.

**Changing the plan at the last minute.** Whatever protocol is agreed upon in the days before the meet, stick to it. Last-minute changes based on how she feels, what she reads online, or what another competitor is doing introduce variables that have not been tested and create anxiety that does not serve her. The plan is the plan.

# Complete 4-Week Powerlifting Peak Block
### Final Integrated Programme — All Adjustments Incorporated

---

## Client Profile and Block Overview

28-year-old female, intermediate recreational lifter, powerlifting meet in 28 days. Twelve weeks of accumulation completed. Final accumulation block was demanding and left significant residual fatigue. This block runs four weeks: a genuine deload to clear that fatigue, a controlled reduction week to begin the intensity ramp, a peak intensity week containing 95% opener confirmation singles and a mock meet simulation, and a final taper week designed to deliver a fully recovered, neurally sharp athlete to the platform on meet day.

Every decision in this block serves one outcome. Walking onto the platform on meet day feeling fast, tight, and confident. The fitness has been built. The job now is to express it.

---

## Governing Principles

**Volume decreases across every week.** From the deload through to meet day, total training volume follows a consistent downward trajectory. There are no exceptions and no weeks where volume creeps back up because things feel good.

**Intensity holds or climbs until Week 3, then pulls back in Week 4.** The weights on the bar do not decrease meaningfully until the taper week. The nervous system needs to stay accustomed to heavy loads throughout the block — only the volume around those loads is reduced.

**The competition lifts are performed to competition standard in every session.** Every squat includes the walk-out, the commands, and the rack. Every bench includes the pause and the press command. Every deadlift includes the full setup ritual. There are no casual reps in this block. Every rep is a rehearsal.

**Accessory work is progressively stripped.** Week 1 carries moderate accessory volume. Week 2 carries minimal accessory work. Week 3 carries almost none. Week 4 carries nothing beyond the competition lifts themselves.

**Rest is training.** Sleep, nutrition, and recovery are not supplementary to this programme — they are central components of it. An athlete who trains perfectly but sleeps six hours a night and eats inconsistently will underperform an athlete who trains adequately and recovers excellently.

---

## Terminology

- **%1RM** — percentage of current training max, typically set at 90–95% of true maximum
- **RPE** — Rate of Perceived Exertion on a 1–10 scale; RPE 8 means approximately two reps remaining
- **Competition lifts** — Squat, Bench Press, Deadlift performed to full competition standard throughout
- **Opener, Second, Third** — planned meet attempts confirmed by end of Week 3

---

## Attempt Selection Framework

Establish these numbers before the block begins. They anchor every percentage across all four weeks.

| Attempt | Guideline | Example at 200 kg training max |
|---|---|---|
| Opener | 90–92% of training max — a guaranteed white-light lift on the worst day imaginable | 180–184 kg |
| Second | 97–100% of training max — a strong, confident performance | 194–200 kg |
| Third | 102–105% of training max — the dream lift | 204–210 kg |

Openers are confirmed after the 95% singles in Week 3. They do not change after that point under any circumstances.
