# WEEK 1 — Deload
### Theme: *Clear the fatigue. Protect the pattern. Do not train hard.*
### Distance from meet: 28–22 days out

The accumulation block was rough. The body is carrying fatigue that will not express itself as fitness on meet day unless it is deliberately cleared. This week does that clearing. Volume drops to approximately 30–35% of the final accumulation week. Intensity stays moderate — nothing above 75–80%. The competition lifts are performed in every session to maintain movement pattern continuity, but the loading is conservative enough that the sessions feel almost easy by the end of the week.

The deload dip is real and worth flagging with your client in advance. Days three and four of this week will likely feel flat, heavy, and psychologically low. This is fatigue clearing, not fitness disappearing. It resolves by days five through seven. If she messages you mid-week saying she feels terrible, the correct response is: this is exactly what is supposed to happen. Keep eating, keep sleeping, trust the process.

**Training frequency: 3 days**

---

### Day 1 — Squat and Deadlift

**Warm-up:** 10 minutes. Hip circles, leg swings front-to-back and side-to-side, goblet squat × 10, thoracic rotation, box breathing. Work up to the bar and add weight in comfortable jumps. Do not abbreviate the warm-up because the session is light — the warm-up serves a different purpose than the working sets.

**Competition Squat**
- 1 × 5 @ 60%
- 1 × 3 @ 70%
- 2 × 2 @ 75%

*Four total working sets. The 75% doubles should feel almost trivially easy. Bar speed is the metric that matters this week more than any percentage. Every rep should move fast. If the doubles feel heavy, the accumulation block left more fatigue than anticipated — note this and keep intensity here for an extra session before progressing into Week 2.*

**Competition Deadlift**
- 1 × 3 @ 60%
- 2 × 2 @ 70%

*Three sets only. Full setup ritual on every rep — stance, grip, brace, pull. The deadlift is the most systemically taxing of the three lifts and receives the most conservative treatment this week.*

**No accessory work.** Session ends after the deadlift sets. Total time including warm-up: 45–55 minutes. If it feels too short, that is correct.

---

### Day 2 — Bench Press

**Warm-up:** Band pull-aparts 2 × 15, shoulder circles, rotator cuff activation with light band — external rotation and face pull pattern, floor press with empty bar. 8–10 minutes.

**Competition Bench Press**
- 1 × 5 @ 60%
- 1 × 3 @ 70%
- 2 × 3 @ 75%

*The bench recovers faster than the squat and deadlift and tolerates slightly higher rep counts at this intensity without meaningful fatigue cost. Three reps at 75% rather than doubles — still well within deload parameters. Every rep paused to competition standard.*

**Regarding the shoulder retraction cue:** she has been cueing herself to pull her shoulders together throughout the accumulation block. Do not drill this, do not correct it, and do not introduce any new language around it this week. Watch the 75% sets on Day 1 of this week specifically. If the upper back position looks solid, the bar path is consistent, and the setup looks fluid rather than forced, the cue has become automatic movement and requires no intervention. Affirm it once — the upper back position looks solid, trust what you have built — and do not raise the subject again until after the meet. If something looks genuinely problematic, the only intervention is a single quiet simplification: set it and forget it, find the position in the setup and then stop thinking about it. Say it once. Do not repeat it as a constant reminder.

**Dumbbell Row**
- 2 × 8 per side @ RPE 5

**Face Pulls**
- 2 × 15 with light band or cable

Session ends. No additional pressing, no tricep work, nothing that adds meaningful fatigue to the pressing pattern.

---

### Day 3 — Full Body, Light

This session exists to maintain movement frequency across all three competition lifts without adding meaningful fatigue. It is the shortest session of the week and should feel almost like an extended warm-up.

**Competition Squat**
- 1 × 3 @ 65%
- 1 × 2 @ 72%

**Competition Bench Press**
- 1 × 3 @ 65%
- 1 × 2 @ 72%

**Competition Deadlift**
- 1 × 3 @ 62%
- 1 × 1 @ 70%

Six working sets across three lifts. Session complete in 35–40 minutes including warm-up. The athlete should leave feeling loose, mobile, and slightly frustrated that she did not do more. That frustration is the deload working.

---

### Week 1 Cardio

All sessions kept at the lower end of prescribed durations. Fatigue clearance is the priority and easy aerobic work supports it. Heart rate ceiling for every cardio session in this entire block: 130–140 bpm. If she cannot hold a full conversation, she is working too hard.

**Rest Day 1 — Walk, 20 minutes.** Easy pace, outdoors if possible. No heart rate target beyond the ceiling above. Move and breathe.

**Rest Day 2 — Stationary bike, 15 minutes.** Low resistance, comfortable cadence. A metabolic flush rather than a cardiovascular session.

**Rest Day 3 — Walk, 15–20 minutes.** The final rest day before Week 2 begins. Keep it easy and use the walk to mentally transition into the peak block mindset.

No post-session bike flushes this week. The sessions are short enough that they do not generate the metabolic byproduct accumulation that makes the flush valuable.

---

### Week 1 Nutrition

Calories remain at or above maintenance. This is not a cut week. The body is actively repairing tissue and consolidating adaptations from the accumulation block — this process requires energy and protein. Cutting calories during a deload is nutritionally equivalent to doing renovation work and turning off the electricity. The materials are there but the tools do not work.

**Protein:** 1.8–2.2 g per kg of bodyweight daily. Non-negotiable throughout the block.

**Carbohydrates:** Moderate to high. Glycogen stores need to be fully replenished after a demanding accumulation block. This takes several days of consistent carbohydrate intake and cannot be rushed by eating more in a single day.

**Fat:** Normal levels.

**Total calories:** Maintenance or slightly above. This is not a body composition week.

If managing weight for a weight class, monitor morning weight daily this week. Note the trend. Plan any necessary adjustments for later in the block. No restriction yet — simply awareness.

**Sleep target: 8–9 hours every night with consistent sleep and wake times.** This is the single most powerful recovery tool available and costs nothing. Irregular sleep schedules — even with adequate total hours — disrupt the hormonal environment that governs recovery.

---

### Week 1 Recovery

Soft tissue work is actively encouraged this week. A sports massage if accessible is an excellent investment — ideally on Day 2 or Day 3 when initial acute soreness from the first session has cleared. Foam rolling and massage gun work on quads, hamstrings, glutes, thoracic spine, and lats for 10–15 minutes daily is beneficial.

Avoid any new physical activities, sports, or recreational activities that carry injury risk. One optional easy walk on any rest day beyond the prescribed cardio is fine. No additional cardio beyond what is programmed.

Begin practising the meet-day morning routine mentally. What she eats, when she warms up, how she handles the platform. Visualisation practice — 5 minutes before sleep, mentally walk through each lift on meet day. The warm-up room, the platform, the commands, the lift, the white lights.

---

### Distance from meet: 21–15 days out

Fatigue should be meaningfully reduced coming out of the deload. Week 2 begins the intensity ramp while keeping volume at approximately 60% of the final accumulation week. ### Week 2 Cardio

**Rest Day between Day 2 and Day 3 — Stationary bike or rower, 20 minutes.** Low resistance, comfortable cadence. Bike preferred if lower back sensitivity is present from deadlift work. Rower excellent for upper back blood flow after bench sessions. Follow with 5 minutes of light dynamic stretching.

**Post-session flush on Day 1 or Day 3 — Stationary bike, 15 minutes immediately following the session.** Low resistance, cadence comfortable, heart rate not exceeding 120 bpm. Legs should feel loosening up, not working harder. Follow with 5 minutes of light stretching.

---

### Week 2 Nutrition

Calories at maintenance or slightly above. Protein remains at 1.8–2.2 g per kg of bodyweight. Carbohydrate intake moderate to high, particularly around training sessions. If managing weight, continue daily morning weight monitoring. No aggressive restriction — awareness only.

**Sleep target: 8–9 hours.**

---

### Week 2 Recovery

# WEEK 3 — Peak Intensity and Opener Confirmation
### Theme: *The heaviest week — 95% singles, confidence-building, mock meet*
### Distance from meet: 14–8 days out

Week 3 is the intensity apex of the block. Volume drops to approximately 40% of the final accumulation week but the weights on the bar are the heaviest the client will touch before meet day. This week contains 95% opener confirmation singles on all three competition lifts distributed across dedicated sessions, followed by a mock meet simulation at reduced intensity. The 95% singles serve two purposes: confirming that the opener is correctly selected, and giving the nervous system a high-intensity stimulus that will supercompensate into meet day.

**Training frequency: 4 days**

A direct conversation about the 95% singles is warranted before this week begins. 95% of training max sits between the opener and the second attempt. It is heavier than the planned opener and approaching the planned second. The fatigue cost is real, the injury risk is elevated compared to 88–92% work, and the psychological information it provides — while valuable — comes at a price that must be consciously accepted. Ask the client what she is specifically trying to confirm. If the answer is that the opener is there, the 92–93% work already in the original programme answers that question with lower risk. If the answer is that she needs to feel a heavy bar before the meet or she will not feel ready, that is a legitimate psychological need — acknowledge it as such, programme accordingly, and make sure she understands the trade-off.

Three rules govern the 95% singles. First, not all three lifts on the same day — the singles are distributed across two sessions with adequate recovery between them. Second, the deadlift receives the most conservative treatment and is programmed last in the week on its own day. Third, if any single looks or feels like RPE 9.5 or above, the remaining singles are reduced to 90–92% or removed. One bad single is information. Pushing through three bad singles is how people get hurt three weeks before a meet.

---

### Day 1 — Squat 95% Single and Bench Moderate
### *(Monday or Tuesday)*

**Warm-up:** Full general warm-up — 10 minutes minimum. Leg swings, hip circles, goblet squat, thoracic rotation. Do not abbreviate this warm-up. The nervous system needs time to arrive before a near-maximal effort.

**Competition Squat — Opener Confirmation Single**

Work up deliberately. Jumps between sets should be comfortable and the bar should feel faster with each warm-up set as the nervous system activates. If the bar is slowing down during the warm-up rather than speeding up, that is a signal worth noting.

- 1 × 5 @ 50%
- 1 × 3 @ 60%
- 1 × 2 @ 70%
- 1 × 1 @ 80%
- 1 × 1 @ 87%
- 1 × 1 @ 92%
- **1 × 1 @ 95% ← Opener confirmation single**

*Rest 4–5 minutes before the 92% single. Rest a full 5 minutes before the 95% single. Do not rush this. The warm-up sets are preparation for the one set that matters.*

**Interpreting the 95% squat single:** Target RPE 8 to 8.5 — one to one and a half reps left in the tank, technically sound, no significant form breakdown. RPE 8 or below confirms the opener and allows the second attempt to be set with confidence. RPE 8.5–9 confirms the opener but the second attempt should be conservative. RPE 9 or above — a genuine grind — have the conversation about whether the opener needs to come down by 2.5–5 kg.

**After the squat single — rest 8–10 minutes before touching the bench bar.** This is longer than a normal inter-exercise rest and it is intentional. The squat single has taxed the entire system and the bench needs a partially recovered nervous system, not one still processing a near-maximal squat.

**Competition Bench Press — Moderate Work**

This is not a heavy bench day. The bench single is coming on Day 2. Today's bench work is moderate intensity maintenance — keeping the pattern fresh without adding meaningful fatigue.

- 1 × 3 @ 70%
- 1 × 2 @ 78%
- 1 × 1 @ 83%

*The 83% single should feel comfortable — RPE 7 at most. If it feels heavier than that, drop it to 80% and note it.*

No accessory work. Session ends after the bench sets. Total session time: 75–90 minutes including warm-up.

---

### Day 2 — Bench 95% Single
### *(Wednesday — at least 48 hours after Day 1)*

# Complete 4-Week Powerlifting Peak Block
### Final Integrated Programme — All Adjustments Incorporated

---

## Client Profile and Block Overview

28-year-old female, intermediate recreational lifter, powerlifting meet in 28 days. Twelve weeks of accumulation completed. Final accumulation block was demanding and left significant residual fatigue. This block runs four weeks: a genuine deload to clear that fatigue, a controlled reduction week to begin the intensity ramp, a peak intensity week containing 95% opener confirmation singles and a mock meet simulation, and a final taper week designed to deliver a fully recovered, neurally sharp athlete to the platform on meet day.

Every decision in this block serves one outcome. Walking onto the platform on meet day feeling fast, tight, and confident. The fitness has been built. The job now is to express it.

---

## Governing Principles

**Volume decreases across every week.** From the deload through to meet day, total training volume follows a consistent downward trajectory. There are no exceptions and no weeks where volume creeps back up because things feel good.

**Intensity holds or climbs until Week 3, then pulls back in Week 4.** The weights on the bar do not decrease meaningfully until the taper week. The nervous system needs to stay accustomed to heavy loads throughout the block — only the volume around those loads is reduced.

**The competition lifts are performed to competition standard in every session.** Every squat includes the walk-out, the commands, and the rack. Every bench includes the pause and the press command. Every deadlift includes the full setup ritual. There are no casual reps in this block. Every rep is a rehearsal.

**Accessory work is progressively stripped.** Week 1 carries moderate accessory volume. Week 2 carries minimal accessory work. Week 3 carries almost none. Week 4 carries nothing beyond the competition lifts themselves.

**Rest is training.** Sleep, nutrition, and recovery are not supplementary to this programme — they are central components of it. An athlete who trains perfectly but sleeps six hours a night and eats inconsistently will underperform an athlete who trains adequately and recovers excellently.

---

## Terminology

- **%1RM** — percentage of current training max, typically set at 90–95% of true maximum
- **RPE** — Rate of Perceived Exertion on a 1–10 scale; RPE 8 means approximately two reps remaining
- **Competition lifts** — Squat, Bench Press, Deadlift performed to full competition standard throughout
- **Opener, Second, Third** — planned meet attempts confirmed by end of Week 3

---

## Attempt Selection Framework

Establish these numbers before the block begins. They anchor every percentage across all four weeks.

| Attempt | Guideline | Example at 200 kg training max |
|---|---|---|
| Opener | 90–92% of training max — a guaranteed white-light lift on the worst day imaginable | 180–184 kg |
| Second | 97–100% of training max — a strong, confident performance | 194–200 kg |
| Third | 102–105% of training max — the dream lift | 204–210 kg |

Openers are confirmed after the 95% singles in Week 3. They do not change after that point under any circumstances.

---

---

# WEEK 1 — Deload
### Theme: *Clear the fatigue. Protect the pattern. Do not train hard.*
### Distance from meet: 28–22 days out

The accumulation block was rough. The body is carrying fatigue that will not express itself as fitness on meet day unless it is deliberately cleared. This week does that clearing. Volume drops to approximately 30–35% of the final accumulation week. Intensity stays moderate — nothing above 75–80%. The competition lifts are performed in every session to maintain movement pattern continuity, but the loading is conservative enough that the sessions feel almost easy by the end of the week.

The deload dip is real and worth flagging with your client in advance. Days three and four of this week will likely feel flat, heavy, and psychologically low. This is fatigue clearing, not fitness disappearing. It resolves by days five through seven. If she messages you mid-week saying she feels terrible, the correct response is: this is exactly what is supposed to happen. Keep eating, keep sleeping, trust the process.

**Training frequency: 3 days**

---

### Day 1 — Squat and Deadlift

**Warm-up:** 10 minutes. Hip circles, leg swings front-to-back and side-to-side, goblet squat × 10, thoracic rotation, box breathing. Work up to the bar and add weight in comfortable jumps. Do not abbreviate the warm-up because the session is light — the warm-up serves a different purpose than the working sets.

**Competition Squat**
- 1 × 5 @ 60%
- 1 × 3 @ 70%
- 2 × 2 @ 75%

*Four total working sets. The 75% doubles should feel almost trivially easy. Bar speed is the metric that matters this week more than any percentage. Every rep should move fast. If the doubles feel heavy, the accumulation block left more fatigue than anticipated — note this and keep intensity here for an extra session before progressing into Week 2.*

**Competition Deadlift**
- 1 × 3 @ 60%
- 2 × 2 @ 70%

*Three sets only. Full setup ritual on every rep — stance, grip, brace, pull. The deadlift is the most systemically taxing of the three lifts and receives the most conservative treatment this week.*

**No accessory work.** Session ends after the deadlift sets. Total time including warm-up: 45–55 minutes. If it feels too short, that is correct.

---

### Day 2 — Bench Press

**Warm-up:** Band pull-aparts 2 × 15, shoulder circles, rotator cuff activation with light band — external rotation and face pull pattern, floor press with empty bar. 8–10 minutes.

**Competition Bench Press**
- 1 × 5 @ 60%
- 1 × 3 @ 70%
- 2 × 3 @ 75%

*The bench recovers faster than the squat and deadlift and tolerates slightly higher rep counts at this intensity without meaningful fatigue cost. Three reps at 75% rather than doubles — still well within deload parameters. Every rep paused to competition standard.*

**Regarding the shoulder retraction cue:** she has been cueing herself to pull her shoulders together throughout the accumulation block. Do not drill this, do not correct it, and do not introduce any new language around it this week. Watch the 75% sets on Day 1 of this week specifically. If the upper back position looks solid, the bar path is consistent, and the setup looks fluid rather than forced, the cue has become automatic movement and requires no intervention. Affirm it once — the upper back position looks solid, trust what you have built — and do not raise the subject again until after the meet. If something looks genuinely problematic, the only intervention is a single quiet simplification: set it and forget it, find the position in the setup and then stop thinking about it. Say it once. Do not repeat it as a constant reminder.

**Dumbbell Row**
- 2 × 8 per side @ RPE 5

**Face Pulls**
- 2 × 15 with light band or cable

Session ends. No additional pressing, no tricep work, nothing that adds meaningful fatigue to the pressing pattern.

---

### Day 3 — Full Body, Light

This session exists to maintain movement frequency across all three competition lifts without adding meaningful fatigue. It is the shortest session of the week and should feel almost like an extended warm-up.

**Competition Squat**
- 1 × 3 @ 65%
- 1 × 2 @ 72%

**Competition Bench Press**
- 1 × 3 @ 65%
- 1 × 2 @ 72%

**Competition Deadlift**
- 1 × 3 @ 62%
- 1 × 1 @ 70%

Six working sets across three lifts. Session complete in 35–40 minutes including warm-up. The athlete should leave feeling loose, mobile, and slightly frustrated that she did not do more. That frustration is the deload working.

---

### Week 1 Cardio

All sessions kept at the lower end of prescribed durations. Fatigue clearance is the priority and easy aerobic work supports it. Heart rate ceiling for every cardio session in this entire block: 130–140 bpm. If she cannot hold a full conversation, she is working too hard.

**Rest Day 1 — Walk, 20 minutes.** Easy pace, outdoors if possible. No heart rate target beyond the ceiling above. Move and breathe.

**Rest Day 2 — Stationary bike, 15 minutes.** Low resistance, comfortable cadence. A metabolic flush rather than a cardiovascular session.

**Rest Day 3 — Walk, 15–20 minutes.** The final rest day before Week 2 begins. Keep it easy and use the walk to mentally transition into the peak block mindset.

No post-session bike flushes this week. The sessions are short enough that they do not generate the metabolic byproduct accumulation that makes the flush valuable.

---

### Week 1 Nutrition

Calories remain at or above maintenance. This is not a cut week. The body is actively repairing tissue and consolidating adaptations from the accumulation block — this process requires energy and protein. Cutting calories during a deload is nutritionally equivalent to doing renovation work and turning off the electricity. The materials are there but the tools do not work.

**Protein:** 1.8–2.2 g per kg of bodyweight daily. Non-negotiable throughout the block.

**Carbohydrates:** Moderate to high. Glycogen stores need to be fully replenished after a demanding accumulation block. This takes several days of consistent carbohydrate intake and cannot be rushed by eating more in a single day.

**Fat:** Normal levels.

**Total calories:** Maintenance or slightly above. This is not a body composition week.

If managing weight for a weight class, monitor morning weight daily this week. Note the trend. Plan any necessary adjustments for later in the block. No restriction yet — simply awareness.

**Sleep target: 8–9 hours every night with consistent sleep and wake times.** This is the single most powerful recovery tool available and costs nothing. Irregular sleep schedules — even with adequate total hours — disrupt the hormonal environment that governs recovery.

---

### Week 1 Recovery

Soft tissue work is actively encouraged this week. A sports massage if accessible is an excellent investment — ideally on Day 2 or Day 3 when initial acute soreness from the first session has cleared. Foam rolling and massage gun work on quads, hamstrings, glutes, thoracic spine, and lats for 10–15 minutes daily is beneficial.

Avoid any new physical activities, sports, or recreational activities that carry injury risk. One optional easy walk on any rest day beyond the prescribed cardio is fine. No additional cardio beyond what is programmed.

Begin practising the meet-day morning routine mentally. What she eats, when she warms up, how she handles the platform. Visualisation practice — 5 minutes before sleep, mentally walk through each lift on meet day. The warm-up room, the platform, the commands, the lift, the white lights.

---

---

# WEEK 2 — Controlled Reduction
### Theme: *Strip the volume, keep the weight moving fast*
### Distance from meet: 21–15 days out

Fatigue should be meaningfully reduced coming out of the deload. Week 2 begins the intensity ramp while keeping volume at approximately 60% of the final accumulation week. Sessions should feel moderately challenging but never grinding. Bar speed should feel noticeably better than it did in the final accumulation weeks. Accessory work is present but reduced.

**Training frequency: 4 days**

---

### Day 1 — Squat Focus

**Warm-up:** 10 minutes general movement — hip circles, leg swings, goblet squat × 10, box breathing. Work up to the bar in comfortable jumps.

**Competition Squat**
- 1 × 5 @ 65%
- 1 × 3 @ 75%
- 3 × 3 @ 80%

*Rest 3–4 minutes between working sets. Focus on competition commands on every rep. Every set is a rehearsal.*

**Pause Squat** (2-second pause in the hole)
- 2 × 3 @ 65%

*Technique and positional tool, not a strength stimulus. Light and deliberate.*

**Romanian Deadlift**
- 3 × 6 @ RPE 6–7

*Posterior chain maintenance. Not a PR attempt.*

**Leg Press**
- 2 × 10 @ moderate load

**Core:** Plank 3 × 30 seconds, Dead Bug 2 × 8 per side

---

### Day 2 — Bench Press Focus

**Warm-up:** Band pull-aparts 2 × 15, shoulder circles, light rotator cuff work, floor press with empty bar.

**Competition Bench Press**
- 1 × 5 @ 65%
- 1 × 3 @ 75%
- 3 × 3 @ 80%

*Pause on the chest on every rep to competition standard. Focus on leg drive, back tightness, and a consistent touch point.*

**Close-Grip Bench Press**
- 2 × 5 @ 65%

**Dumbbell Row**
- 3 × 8 per side @ RPE 6

**Face Pulls**
- 3 × 15 with light cable or band

**Tricep Pushdown**
- 2 × 12 @ light load

---

### Day 3 — Deadlift Focus

**Warm-up:** Hip hinge patterning — kettlebell deadlift × 10, band-resisted hip extension × 10, hamstring stretch.

**Competition Deadlift**
- 1 × 5 @ 65%
- 1 × 3 @ 75%
- 3 × 3 @ 80%

*Pull from the floor with full setup ritual on every rep.*

**Deficit Deadlift** (1–2 inch deficit)
- 2 × 3 @ 65%

*Off-the-floor strength and positional awareness. Light and technical.*

**Leg Curl**
- 3 × 8

**Lat Pulldown**
- 3 × 10 @ moderate load

**Core:** Pallof Press 3 × 10 per side

---

### Day 4 — Upper Body and Bench Variation

**Competition Bench Press**
- 1 × 3 @ 75%
- 2 × 2 @ 82%

*Slightly higher intensity than Day 2 to begin the intensity ramp. Short and sharp.*

**Overhead Press**
- 3 × 6 @ RPE 6

**Cable Row**
- 3 × 10

**Dumbbell Lateral Raise**
- 2 × 15

**Bicep Curl**
- 2 × 12

---

### Week 2 Cardio

**Rest Day between Day 1 and Day 2 — Walk, 25 minutes.** Brisk walking outdoors or treadmill at 5.5–6.5 km/h with 2–3% incline. Blood flow, cortisol regulation, taper anxiety management.

**Rest Day between Day 2 and Day 3 — Stationary bike or rower, 20 minutes.** Low resistance, comfortable cadence. Bike preferred if lower back sensitivity is present from deadlift work. Rower excellent for upper back blood flow after bench sessions. Follow with 5 minutes of light dynamic stretching.

**Post-session flush on Day 1 or Day 3 — Stationary bike, 15 minutes immediately following the session.** Low resistance, cadence comfortable, heart rate not exceeding 120 bpm. Legs should feel loosening up, not working harder. Follow with 5 minutes of light stretching.

---

### Week 2 Nutrition

Calories at maintenance or slightly above. Protein remains at 1.8–2.2 g per kg of bodyweight. Carbohydrate intake moderate to high, particularly around training sessions. If managing weight, continue daily morning weight monitoring. No aggressive restriction — awareness only.

**Sleep target: 8–9 hours.**

---

### Week 2 Recovery

Soft tissue work permitted and encouraged — 10 minutes post-session on quads, hamstrings, glutes, and upper back. Avoid deep tissue work on the day before a heavy session. Continue visualisation practice nightly.

---

---

# WEEK 3 — Peak Intensity and Opener Confirmation
### Theme: *The heaviest week — 95% singles, confidence-building, mock meet*
### Distance from meet: 14–8 days out

Week 3 is the intensity apex of the block. Volume drops to approximately 40% of the final accumulation week but the weights on the bar are the heaviest the client will touch before meet day. This week contains 95% opener confirmation singles on all three competition lifts distributed across dedicated sessions, followed by a mock meet simulation at reduced intensity. The 95% singles serve two purposes: confirming that the opener is correctly selected, and giving the nervous system a high-intensity stimulus that will supercompensate into meet day.

**Training frequency: 4 days**

A direct conversation about the 95% singles is warranted before this week begins. 95% of training max sits between the opener and the second attempt. It is heavier than the planned opener and approaching the planned second. The fatigue cost is real, the injury risk is elevated compared to 88–92% work, and the psychological information it provides — while valuable — comes at a price that must be consciously accepted. Ask the client what she is specifically trying to confirm. If the answer is that the opener is there, the 92–93% work already in the original programme answers that question with lower risk. If the answer is that she needs to feel a heavy bar before the meet or she will not feel ready, that is a legitimate psychological need — acknowledge it as such, programme accordingly, and make sure she understands the trade-off.

Three rules govern the 95% singles. First, not all three lifts on the same day — the singles are distributed across two sessions with adequate recovery between them. Second, the deadlift receives the most conservative treatment and is programmed last in the week on its own day. Third, if any single looks or feels like RPE 9.5 or above, the remaining singles are reduced to 90–92% or removed. One bad single is information. Pushing through three bad singles is how people get hurt three weeks before a meet.

---

### Day 1 — Squat 95% Single and Bench Moderate
### *(Monday or Tuesday)*

**Warm-up:** Full general warm-up — 10 minutes minimum. Leg swings, hip circles, goblet squat, thoracic rotation. Do not abbreviate this warm-up. The nervous system needs time to arrive before a near-maximal effort.

**Competition Squat — Opener Confirmation Single**

Work up deliberately. Jumps between sets should be comfortable and the bar should feel faster with each warm-up set as the nervous system activates. If the bar is slowing down during the warm-up rather than speeding up, that is a signal worth noting.

- 1 × 5 @ 50%
- 1 × 3 @ 60%
- 1 × 2 @ 70%
- 1 × 1 @ 80%
- 1 × 1 @ 87%
- 1 × 1 @ 92%
- **1 × 1 @ 95% ← Opener confirmation single**

*Rest 4–5 minutes before the 92% single. Rest a full 5 minutes before the 95% single. Do not rush this. The warm-up sets are preparation for the one set that matters.*

**Interpreting the 95% squat single:** Target RPE 8 to 8.5 — one to one and a half reps left in the tank, technically sound, no significant form breakdown. RPE 8 or below confirms the opener and allows the second attempt to be set with confidence. RPE 8.5–9 confirms the opener but the second attempt should be conservative. RPE 9 or above — a genuine grind — have the conversation about whether the opener needs to come down by 2.5–5 kg.

**After the squat single — rest 8–10 minutes before touching the bench bar.** This is longer than a normal inter-exercise rest and it is intentional. The squat single has taxed the entire system and the bench needs a partially recovered nervous system, not one still processing a near-maximal squat.

**Competition Bench Press — Moderate Work**

This is not a heavy bench day. The bench single is coming on Day 2. Today's bench work is moderate intensity maintenance — keeping the pattern fresh without adding meaningful fatigue.

- 1 × 3 @ 70%
- 1 × 2 @ 78%
- 1 × 1 @ 83%

*The 83% single should feel comfortable — RPE 7 at most. If it feels heavier than that, drop it to 80% and note it.*

No accessory work. Session ends after the bench sets. Total session time: 75–90 minutes including warm-up.

---

### Day 2 — Bench 95% Single
### *(Wednesday — at least 48 hours after Day 1)*

The bench gets its own dedicated day. Upper body recovers faster than lower body but giving the bench single a dedicated session means it can be approached fresh and treated with the same seriousness as the squat single.

**Warm-up:** Band pull-aparts 2 × 15, shoulder circles, rotator cuff activation, floor press with empty bar. 8–10 minutes.

**Competition Bench Press — Opener Confirmation Single**

- 1 × 5 @ 50%
- 1 × 3 @ 62%
- 1 × 2 @ 72%
- 1 × 1 @ 80%
- 1 × 1 @ 87%
- 1 × 1 @ 92%
- **1 × 1 @ 95% ← Opener confirmation single**

*Rest 3–4 minutes between lighter sets. Rest a full 4–5 minutes before the 92% and 95% singles. Every rep from 80% onwards performed to full competition standard — pause on the chest, wait for the press command, full lockout, wait for the rack command. No touch-and-go, no abbreviated pauses.*

**Interpreting the 95% bench single:** Same RPE framework as the squat. Pay particular attention to the pause and the press command. Meet nerves sometimes cause lifters to jump the press command in competition and a heavy single in training is a good opportunity to reinforce the habit of waiting. If the pause feels long and uncomfortable at 95%, that is normal and will feel shorter on the platform with adrenaline running.

**Close-Grip Bench Press**
- 2 × 3 @ 65%

**Face Pulls**
- 2 × 15

Session ends. 50–65 minutes total.

---

### Day 3 — Deadlift 95% Single
### *(Friday — at least 48 hours after Day 2)*

The deadlift single gets the most space of the three. It stands alone with nothing else of consequence in the session. The deadlift is the lift that most commonly causes problems when pushed too hard too close to a meet — lower back fatigue, grip fatigue, and general systemic stress all accumulate here in a way they do not with the other two lifts.

**Warm-up:** Hip hinge patterning — kettlebell deadlift × 10, band-resisted hip extension × 10, hamstring stretch. 8 minutes.

**Competition Deadlift — Opener Confirmation Single**

- 1 × 3 @ 50%
- 1 × 2 @ 62%
- 1 × 1 @ 72%
- 1 × 1 @ 80%
- 1 × 1 @ 87%
- 1 × 1 @ 92%
- **1 × 1 @ 95% ← Opener confirmation single**

*Rest 4–5 minutes before the 87% single. Rest a full 5–6 minutes before the 92% single. Rest a full 6 minutes before the 95% single. Deadlift warm-up rests are longer than squat and bench rests because the posterior chain and lower back need more time between near-maximal efforts.*
